sub_unit_name: Introduction to hardness of water - Estimation of hardness of water by complexometric method and related numerical problems

content.title: What is Hardness of Water?
content.description: Hardness of water is the property caused by dissolved calcium (Ca²⁺) and magnesium (Mg²⁺) salts, which reduce the ability of water to form lather with soap.

content.content: Hard water contains dissolved minerals, mainly calcium and magnesium ions. These ions react with soap to form insoluble precipitates, reducing soap efficiency. Hardness is generally expressed in terms of mg/L (ppm) as CaCO₃.

content.title: Why Study Water Hardness?
content.content: Knowledge of water hardness is important in domestic, industrial, and boiler applications to prevent scaling, improve cleaning efficiency, and ensure safe water usage.

Water hardness is classified into temporary hardness and permanent hardness. Temporary hardness is caused by bicarbonates of calcium and magnesium, while permanent hardness is caused by chlorides and sulphates.

items.question: Soap Consumption
items.answer: Hard water consumes more soap before lather is produced.

items.question: Scaling
items.answer: Scale deposits form in boilers, pipes, and heat exchangers.

items.question: Reduced Heating Efficiency
items.answer: Scale acts as an insulator and increases fuel consumption.

items.question: Industrial Problems
items.answer: Hard water affects textile, paper, pharmaceutical, and food industries.

content.content: The complexometric titration method uses EDTA (Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid) to estimate total hardness of water. EDTA forms stable complexes with calcium and magnesium ions.

content.title: Principle of EDTA Titration
content.description: EDTA reacts with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions in a 1:1 ratio to form stable, colorless complexes. The amount of EDTA consumed indicates the hardness of water.

content.title: EDTA Titration Steps
steps: Observe Wine Red to Blue Color Change

content.content: Eriochrome Black T (EBT) forms a wine-red complex with metal ions. During titration, EDTA binds with calcium and magnesium ions, releasing the indicator and producing a blue color at the end point.

content.title: Easy Analogy
content.content: Imagine EDTA as a magnet that attracts calcium and magnesium ions away from the indicator. Once all ions are captured, the indicator changes from red to blue, signaling the end of the titration.
Total Hardness (mg/L as CaCO₃) = (Volume of EDTA × Strength of EDTA × 1000) / Volume of Water Sample

content.title: Unit
content.content: Water hardness is commonly expressed as mg/L or ppm (parts per million) as CaCO₃.

Problem: 25 mL of water requires 10 mL of 1 mg/mL EDTA solution. Calculate total hardness.

Solution:
Total Hardness = (10 × 1 × 1000) / 25 = 400 mg/L (400 ppm as CaCO₃).

items.question: Industries
items.answer: Maintain product quality and equipment life.

content.title: Limitations of EDTA Method
content.content: The method requires proper pH maintenance and careful endpoint observation. Presence of interfering metal ions may affect the accuracy.

content.title: Remember This
content.description: EDTA forms a 1:1 complex with calcium and magnesium ions. The amount of EDTA required is directly proportional to the hardness of water.
